name: Aaron Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a drummer, so my day starts late and ends late. Three afternoons a week I teach drums in a soundproofed room at the back of a music shop, mostly teenagers and a couple of dads who've decided to finally learn. When a touring musical comes to town I'm in the pit at the city theatre, eight shows a week for three or four weeks. Saturdays I play in a country covers band at a roadhouse out on the highway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the pit, the way thirty seconds of silence turns into a big entrance and the whole crowd jumps. What wears me out is my back, hauling a kit in and out of venues, and the gaps between musicals when the theatre doesn't need me for two months. My girlfriend Hanna teaches at a primary school, and we're saving for a house deposit. I use AI now and then, mostly to write up lesson plans, but I'm not a gadget guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's about what I'd guess, honestly. Lots of noise, a few new gadgets, then back to normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never bought the hype and I'm glad I didn't panic. At the shop we'd joke that the robots couldn't keep time anyway. I wouldn't say much online; I mostly post drum covers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry was never AI, it's backing tracks. Touring shows have been cutting pit bands for years, swapping players for a laptop with pre-recorded parts. Last spring a show came through with a four-piece pit instead of seven, and I only got the job because their drummer quit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the three things going and keep putting four hundred dollars a month into the house fund. I'd try to pick up another regular night, maybe a hotel lounge gig on Thursdays. And I'd keep using the AI to make play-along tracks for my students, because it saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little itch about the pit work, but that itch was there before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a gap between musicals do to your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It knocks about a third off my month. Two months without a show last winter meant the house fund got nothing from me, and Hanna kept saving while I didn't, which I didn't love. My dad always said a man pays his own way, and I still believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the theatre would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The string players, more than me. When producers cut a theatre pit band, the violins and cello go first because a keyboard can fake them. A drummer is hard to fake live, because the actors follow the drums, so I'm usually the last one standing.

say: I **never bought the hype** and I'm glad I didn't panic.
At the shop we'd **joke** that robots couldn't keep time anyway.
think: My real worry is **backing tracks**, not AI, because pit bands keep shrinking.
A show last spring used a **four-piece pit** instead of seven players.
do: Keep all **three jobs** going and save four hundred dollars a month for a house.
Try to add a **Thursday lounge gig** at a hotel.
Keep using AI for **play-along tracks**, saving about an hour a week.
feel: **Fine, mostly**, with an itch about pit work that predates AI.
S0.quote: When producers cut a theatre pit band, the violins and cello go first because a keyboard can fake them.
fieldNote: Aaron's pressure comes from **shrinking pit bands**, driven by cost-cutting producers, not AI.
He takes **pride** in paying his own way and dislikes falling behind his girlfriend's savings.
He sees the drummer as **hardest to fake** live, a quiet source of confidence.

steps.text: Keep teaching, pit work and Saturday roadhouse gigs going
Put four hundred dollars a month into the house deposit fund
Pick up a regular Thursday hotel lounge gig

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That feels like the one that's actually coming, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say live drums still need a drummer, and that's true. At the shop I'd tell the parents that learning a real instrument matters more than ever. I'd keep the tone practical, not doom and gloom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the pit is where it hurts. If AI can make a full orchestra track that follows the actors and changes speed on the night, the producers will cut us down to a keyboard player and a conductor. The studio work, recording drums for local bands at a friend's place, goes too, maybe two thousand dollars a year. And the shop's owner already asked me whether an app could do beginner lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the shop owner's question seriously and offer to build a beginner course that uses an app at home plus a lesson with me every other week, so the shop keeps the students and I keep the hours. I'd start using AI more for practice plans, once I see other teachers doing it well. And I'd ask my uncle about an apprenticeship, because a trade on the side wouldn't hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've got a bit saved and Hanna's job is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of trade are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's an electrician, and he's said for years I'd be good at it: steady hands, and I'm good with wiring from all the stage gear. He'd take me on as a part-time apprentice, I think. I'd rather learn a trade from a man who's done it thirty years than sit in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off using AI until others do it well. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen guys jump on every new gadget and waste money. I bought an electronic kit five years ago because everyone said it was the future, and it sits in the garage. I'll move when I see a teacher I respect doing it and the students sticking around.

say: **Live drums** still need a drummer, and that's simply true.
Learning a **real instrument** matters more than ever, I'd tell parents at the shop.
think: The **pit** is where it hurts, cut to a keyboard player and a conductor.
Studio drum work, about **two thousand dollars** a year, goes too.
do: Offer the shop a **beginner course** mixing an app with lessons every other week.
Use AI for **practice plans** once I see other teachers doing it well.
Ask my uncle about a part-time **electrician apprenticeship**.
feel: **Anxious but not frozen**, with some savings and Hanna's solid job behind me.
S1.quote: I bought an electronic kit five years ago because everyone said it was the future, and it sits in the garage.
fieldNote: Aaron adopts tech **once proven**; an unused electronic kit taught him caution.
He prefers **apprenticeship** learning from an experienced tradesman over classrooms.
His instinct is to **protect the shop's students** by blending the app with his lessons.

steps.text: Build a beginner course mixing an app with fortnightly lessons at the shop
Use AI to write student practice plans once other teachers do
Ask his uncle about a part-time electrician apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and people should look after their own, family first. At the roadhouse I'd say people will still want a band on a Saturday night, and I'd believe it. I wouldn't moan about it online; there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the pit is finished within a year, because producers will be the first to grab anything that saves wages. The shop's beginner students go to the app, and the shop might close, since it sells to hobbyists who'd have less money. That's two of my three jobs, about two-thirds of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd call my uncle and start the electrician apprenticeship straight away, even at apprentice pay. Electricians do hands-on work, and the robots come about 2031, so that's a few years of work at least, longer if robots are slow getting into old houses. I'd pause the house fund, put everything into an emergency pot, and keep the Saturday roadhouse gig because it's cash and it keeps me playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the night a show closes early and you pack the kit up for the last time and nobody says much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanna about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we wait, and that I'm sorry. Hanna would say a house can wait but we can't, which is her way of saying let's not put off getting married. We'd probably marry at the registry office and skip the big party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hanna's a teacher. Is her job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine, I think. Parents still want an adult in the room with twenty six-year-olds, and robots aren't there until 2031 anyway. But the paperwork side of her job, planning and marking, the AI eats that, so maybe her school hires fewer teachers.

say: It'll be **rough**, and people should look after their own, **family first**.
People will still want **a Saturday night band**, I'd say at the roadhouse.
think: The **pit is finished** within a year, because producers grab anything that saves wages.
Losing pit and shop work means about **two-thirds** of my income goes.
do: Start the **electrician apprenticeship** with my uncle straight away, even at apprentice pay.
**Pause the house fund** and move everything into an emergency pot.
Keep the **Saturday roadhouse** gig for cash and to keep playing.
feel: **Gutted**, like packing up the kit when a show closes early.
S2.quote: First thing, I'd call my uncle and start the electrician apprenticeship straight away, even at apprentice pay.
fieldNote: Two years pushes Aaron straight into a **hands-on trade**, which robots reach later.
He blames **producers** for cutting wages rather than the technology itself.
He'd **marry sooner** and smaller, putting the house aside.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle at apprentice pay
Pause the house fund and build an emergency pot instead
Marry Hanna at the registry office and skip the big party

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32. That's a lot more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone willing to work for it. In the band we'd say get a trade and keep the drums, and that's the plan. I'd tell my students to keep playing for the love of it, not as a whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd still lose the pit and most of the shop teaching, but I'd see it coming. Five years means I can do the apprenticeship properly, four years, and come out qualified right when AGI lands. Then the robots come about 2034, and I'd have a few years as a full electrician before that question even starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd sign on with my uncle for the full four-year apprenticeship, two days a week at first, and keep the pit work when shows come through. I'd keep the house fund going at a smaller rate, two hundred a month instead of four. I'd keep teaching at the shop as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. It's like getting the setlist a week early instead of being handed it at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it feel like giving up on music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. My dad played drums in a covers band every weekend for thirty years and worked as a mechanic all week, and he was happy. I used to think I'd do better than that and make it on music alone. Now I think my dad had it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, just later and smaller, maybe a two-bedroom near Hanna's school so she can walk. Hanna would want a garden for kids someday, and I'd want a garage for the drums. We'd probably have to choose one.

say: Five years is **enough time** for anyone willing to work for it.
Get **a trade** and keep the drums, I'd tell the band and my students.
think: I'd still lose **the pit** and most shop teaching, but I'd see it coming.
A **four-year apprenticeship** finishes right as AGI lands, before robots arrive.
do: Sign on for the **full apprenticeship**, two days a week at first.
Cut the house fund to **two hundred a month** but keep it going.
Keep **teaching and pit work** as long as they'll have me.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, like getting the setlist a week early.
S3.quote: My dad played drums in a covers band every weekend for thirty years and worked as a mechanic all week, and he was happy.
fieldNote: Aaron's model is his **father**: a weekend drummer with a steady trade.
The timing appeals: the apprenticeship **ends as AGI arrives**, before robots in 2034.
His house plans **shrink** rather than disappear, a choice between garden and garage.

steps.text: Sign on for a four-year electrician apprenticeship, two days a week
Keep pit shows and shop teaching alongside the apprenticeship
Buy a smaller two-bedroom house near Hanna's school, later

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Probably a dad by then, if Hanna has her way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years' notice; if you're not ready, that's on you. I'd say that at the roadhouse and mean it, though maybe not to the older guys in the band. Families and churches should help young people get started in a trade, because that's how it's always worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me, but the next few years are still shaky, because the pit and the studio work are already shrinking before AGI even shows up. The money squeeze comes early even if the big change comes late. And we'd want a house and a kid inside those ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two and watch what happens at the theatre before signing up for anything. I'd keep saving four hundred a month for the house, and maybe start the apprenticeship in year two or three, once I can see where it's going. I'd learn the AI tools properly once the teachers at the shop are using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, and sharper when a show comes through with fewer players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your plan is to wait a year or two. What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the next musical at the theatre comes through with a laptop instead of a drummer, I'd ring my uncle the next morning. I'm not a guy who jumps, but I'm not a guy who sits there while the boat sinks either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'that's on you' about people who aren't ready. Does that include you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Yeah, it includes me, which is why I'd keep one eye on it. Saying it out loud is easy; it's harder when the shop's paying me and nobody's told me to stop.

say: With **ten years' notice**, if you're not ready, that's on you.
**Families and churches** should help young people start a trade, as they always have.
think: Ten years is enough for me, but **the squeeze comes early** in pit and studio work.
We'd want a **house and a kid** inside those ten years.
do: **Wait** a year or two and watch what the theatre does first.
Keep saving **four hundred a month** for the house.
Start the **apprenticeship** in year two or three if things look bad.
feel: **Uneasy most days**, and sharper when a show arrives with fewer players.
S4.quote: If the next musical at the theatre comes through with a laptop instead of a drummer, I'd ring my uncle the next morning.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Aaron **wait**, matching his habit of moving once things are proven.
When challenged, he admits **that's on you** applies to him as well.
His trigger is concrete: a **laptop replacing** the drummer in the next musical.
His mood stays anxious because **pit work shrinks** before AGI, while he saves for a house.

steps.text: Watch the next two musicals at the theatre before signing up
Keep saving four hundred dollars a month for the house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years means I'd be a 29-year-old apprentice on apprentice pay with no house, and that's not where I want to be. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage to people retraining in their late twenties, maybe with the government covering part of it for the employer. Not a cheque for sitting at home, a wage for learning a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people actually go to see. Nobody buys a ticket to a musical to hear a laptop. If producers keep cutting the band, eventually audiences notice the show feels thin, and I'd like someone to ask them before the decision gets made.

headlineQuote: Nobody buys a ticket to a musical to hear a laptop.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old drummer** working theatre pits, shop lessons and a Saturday roadhouse band.
He and Hanna, a primary teacher, are **saving for a house** at four hundred dollars a month.
He picks up technology **once it's proven**, after an electronic kit gathered dust.
His backup in every fast scenario is an **electrician apprenticeship** with his uncle.
He blames **cost-cutting producers** and hopes audiences still want a live band.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: a 29-year-old on apprentice pay with no house.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people retraining in their late twenties, partly funded by government.
A **wage for learning** a trade, not a cheque for staying home.
